title: Worksheet — Biodiversity Register (Class 6 CBSE Vocational Education)
instructions: Attempt all 11 questions. Show your reasoning where required. Total time: 50 minutes.

questions.question: Biodiversity means:
options: the variety of life on Earth
questions.answer: the variety of life on Earth

questions.question: Different breeds of cattle are an example of:
It is fine to catch insects and bring them home for closer study.
Earthworms are usually found in the ____ habitat.
When is the BEST time of day to observe BIRDS?
questions.explanation: Birds are most active at dawn.

questions.question: If you are not sure what species you saw, the BEST entry is:
options: guess and write a definite name
write what you saw plus 'possibly X'
questions.answer: write what you saw plus 'possibly X'

questions.question: Define biodiversity and explain its three levels with one example each.
questions.answer: Biodiversity is the variety of life on Earth. Three levels: (i) SPECIES diversity — different KINDS (mango vs neem). (ii) GENETIC diversity — different VARIETIES within one species (basmati vs sona masoori rice). (iii) ECOSYSTEM diversity — different KINDS OF PLACES (forest, river, desert, coral reef).

questions.question: List the SIX things a good biodiversity-register entry should include.
questions.answer: (i) Place — exact location. (ii) Habitat — what the place is like. (iii) Living thing — name (local + scientific if known). (iv) Description — colour, size, behaviour. (v) Date and time. (vi) Source / notes (and honest 'possibly X' if not sure).

questions.question: List FOUR principles of GOOD field observation.
questions.answer: (i) Look quietly for at least 2–3 minutes; let the living thing forget you. (ii) Sketch and describe — colour, size, behaviour. (iii) Record place, time and weather. (iv) Be HONEST about uncertainty. (v) Never catch, hurt or remove living things. (Any four.)

questions.question: Plan how you and your group will run a 4-week BIODIVERSITY REGISTER project at your school. Include: (i) which habitats you will cover, (ii) when you will visit, (iii) what tools you will carry, (iv) what each register entry will contain, (v) how you will share findings.
questions.answer: (i) HABITATS — split the campus into six zones: trees and bushes, ground/leaf-litter, walls and stones, soil, the pond/water tank if any, and the air. Each pair takes one zone. (ii) WHEN — visit 3 times a week for 4 weeks; vary the time-of-day: early morning for birds, noon for insects, after rain for snails and frogs. (iii) TOOLS — small notebook, pencil, magnifying glass, measuring tape, simple field guide, phone for photos with permission. (iv) ENTRY — place, habitat, living-thing name (local + scientific if known), date, time, weather, sketch, colour/size/behaviour, source of identification, 'possibly X' if not sure. (v) SHARING — at week 4, a poster for the corridor and a 5-slide presentation; pick three favourite living things and tell a one-minute story for each; raise three open questions for the school.

questions.question: Suppose your school is planning to cut down an old peepal tree because it 'casts too much shade'. Use ideas from this chapter to argue, with evidence, that the tree should be kept.
questions.answer: I would use the school biodiversity register as evidence. Over the past 4 weeks our register shows the peepal tree alone hosts at least 12 different living things — sparrows, mynas, butterflies, ants, lichens, even a small gecko. The tree is also a pollinator stop for bees. If we cut it, we lose all those species at once and the small ecosystem services they give: bees pollinate kitchen-garden brinjals, birds eat insects, the tree itself cools the playground. Across India, frog and butterfly populations have shrunk because such habitats are cleared. Instead of cutting the tree, I would propose: (a) trim the lower branches to reduce unwanted shade, (b) keep the tree as a 'biodiversity corner' for next year's projects, (c) plant a smaller tree nearby. Conservation does not always mean 'never change' — it means changing thoughtfully, after looking at the evidence we have collected.
questions.explanation: Use register evidence + ecosystem services + alternative.
